title: Mind the Belief Gap
gist: A BCG survey of 563 senior leaders across 11 markets finds 63% believe their senior leadership is not prepared for what long-term success requires, and that the single highest-leverage intervention is not training or systems but reframing the team's shared unexamined assumptions — leaders who actively reframe beliefs are 168% more likely to outperform competitors. The piece uses Hubert Joly's Best Buy turnaround and Ginni Rometty's IBM reinvention to argue that installed systems revert to old behavior unless the belief moves first, and that the largest capability gaps (empathy, clarity) are belief problems, not skill problems.

themes.theme: The Belief Gap as a Diagnostic

insights.claim: BCG defines the 'belief gap' as the distance between what a leadership team knows good leadership requires and what it can actually get itself to do, and argues it closes only when the team collectively surfaces its running assumptions, tests which still fit, and changes the ones that don't.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete diagnostic for management-quality assessment: ask whether a leadership team has ever formally tested its operating assumptions, not whether it has a leadership program.
insights.quote: the distance between what a leadership team knows good leadership requires and what it can actually get itself to do
insights.locator: Reframing beliefs is the hardest of the three

insights.claim: A team's real beliefs are revealed by how it spends time, what it does under pressure, and how it reacts to failure — not by its stated values, which routinely contradict the working assumptions the team actually runs on.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Practical due-diligence heuristic: ignore stated values decks and read time allocation, crisis behavior, and post-mortem conduct as the true signal of culture.
insights.quote: The working assumptions, not the stated values, are what a team runs on.
insights.locator: Belief Comes First

insights.claim: An unexamined belief held by one executive is a personal blind spot, but the same belief held across an entire leadership team becomes a hard ceiling on what the organization believes is possible — meaning individual executive coaching cannot fix a team-level constraint.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Argues the leadership-development spend aimed at individuals is misallocated; the addressable unit is the team, which reframes how to value corporate L&D and coaching vendors.
insights.quote: When one leader holds an unexamined belief, it’s a personal blind spot. When a whole leadership team shares one, it becomes a ceiling to what the organization thinks is possible.
insights.locator: One Mind Isn’t Enough

insights.claim: A single leader who changes her mind will be pulled back to old behavior if she returns to a team whose shared assumptions haven't moved, so reframing succeeds mainly on teams drawn from different backgrounds and skills where dissent is welcome and stalls where unspoken norms suppress new ideas.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Implies that a single high-profile external CEO hire into a homogeneous, consensus-bound top team is a low-probability turnaround bet.
insights.quote: A single leader can change what she believes, but if she walks back into a team whose shared assumptions haven’t moved, the old behavior will pull her back.
insights.locator: One Mind Isn’t Enough

insights.claim: Complaints leadership teams make about unclear expectations, lack of strategic clarity, and inadequate attention to learning look like process problems but each sits on an unquestioned assumption — most commonly the belief that leadership development is separate from the real work.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Warns that fixing the named process complaint (more offsites, clearer OKRs) without moving the belief produces no durable behavior change and wasted transformation budget.
insights.quote: You can hardwire every system you want, but if the team’s shared belief hasn’t shifted, behavior reverts to its previous norms.
insights.locator: In many cases, shared assumptions that a team

themes.theme: Survey Math: Reframing Beats Practice and Systems

insights.claim: In a BCG survey of 563 senior leaders across 11 markets, 63% said the senior leaders in their organization are not well prepared for what long-term success will require.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A near two-thirds internal no-confidence rate in leadership readiness is a base-rate to apply skeptically to any management team pitching a decade-long strategy.
insights.locator: In a recent BCG survey of 563 senior leaders

insights.claim: BCG identifies exactly three mechanisms by which a leadership team adapts to market demands — reframe the beliefs leaders hold, practice new behavior deliberately, and hardwire the new behavior into how the team runs — but only 15% of surveyed leaders do all three consistently.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The 15% completion rate defines the size of the differentiated cohort: adaptive leadership is a rare, potentially mispriced attribute rather than table stakes.
insights.locator: A leadership team grows, evolves, and adapts

insights.claim: Leaders who actively reframe beliefs are 168% more likely to outperform their competitors — a larger measured effect than deliberate practice or hardwiring behavior on its own, making belief work the highest-leverage of the three adaptation mechanisms.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: If replicable, it says the ROI ranking of transformation spend is inverted from practice: most budgets go to training and systems, the smallest-effect levers.
insights.locator: Of the three, one carries disproportionate weight

insights.claim: BCG reports that teams doing all three of reframing, deliberate practice, and hardwiring are '144% as likely' as competitors to outperform and '75% as likely' to report strong long-term preparedness — a stat pairing that reads internally inconsistent, since 75% as likely would imply worse preparedness than peers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Treat the headline multipliers as directional, not precise; the 'as likely' vs 'more likely' phrasing shifts across the piece and the preparedness figure appears mis-stated.
insights.quote: 144% as likely as their competitors to outperform and 75% as likely to report strong long-term preparedness
insights.locator: The survey also found a sharp split

insights.claim: The two things leaders most often credit for their own growth — having a growth mindset (63%) and embracing discomfort and uncertainty (51%) — are not capabilities at all but assumptions leaders hold about themselves, which is why they resist training-based intervention.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reclassifying the top-cited growth drivers as beliefs rather than skills undercuts the premise of most competency-based leadership curricula.
insights.locator: Consider the two things that leaders most often credit

themes.theme: Empathy and Clarity: Execution Gaps, Not Skill Gaps

insights.claim: 41% of senior leaders name empathy a top-three leadership quality but only 16% say senior leaders in their organization excel at it — a 25-percentage-point gap, with clarity showing a 22-point gap, meaning teams fall shortest precisely on the qualities they rank highest.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The say-do gap concentrates on the two qualities most correlated with retention and change execution — a measurable leading indicator of transformation failure.
insights.locator: Empathy is the clearest case

insights.claim: The empathy and clarity shortfalls are not skill deficits but perceived-cost beliefs: leaders assume real empathy would erode their team's accountability and that admitting uncertainty would cost them authority.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Explains why empathy training reliably fails — it addresses capability when the binding constraint is a perceived tradeoff, so remediation must target the tradeoff assumption.
insights.quote: These gaps don’t signal a lack of skill. They come from believing that using these qualities would cost them something.
insights.locator: These gaps don’t signal a lack of skill

insights.claim: The list of qualities senior leaders say matter — empathy, clarity, courage, vision, and cross-boundary 'superteaming' — has remained strikingly stable across BCG's leadership research, confirming that the leadership deficit is a performance problem rather than a knowledge problem.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Stability of the wish-list over years means new leadership frameworks add little; the differentiator is execution, so weight observed behavior over stated leadership philosophy.
insights.quote: This is not a knowledge problem.
insights.locator: Leaders Know What Good Looks Like

themes.theme: Best Buy Turnaround Mechanics Under Joly

insights.claim: When Hubert Joly became CEO of Best Buy in 2012, he rejected the external explanations for decline — consumers moving online, Apple opening its own stores, device convergence — on the logic that the same forces were helping Amazon and Apple, concluding 'we must be the problem.'
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A reusable test for management credibility: if the cited headwind is also a tailwind for a competitor, the attribution is internal, and the turnaround is controllable.
insights.quote: The wind is probably not the problem. We must be the problem.
insights.locator: But Joly was not convinced that these headwinds

insights.claim: Joly's first move at Best Buy was not a strategy offsite but a week working in stores wearing a 'CEO in training' badge and asking employees three questions — what's working, what's not, and what do you need — shifting his view toward less talking from the top and more doing based on what the floor already knew.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Concrete, low-cost diagnostic pattern; frontline immersion before strategy is a tell that a new CEO is sourcing ground truth rather than confirming a thesis.
insights.quote: wearing a “CEO in training” badge and asking employees three questions: what’s working, what’s not, and what do you need?
insights.locator: Joly’s own instinct fit a similar pattern

insights.claim: Best Buy's underlying pre-turnaround belief was that value creation is a zero-sum contest both internally between departments and externally with suppliers, and Joly attacked it by putting every officer on a single set of goals and a single bonus tied to overall company performance under 'one team, one dream, one Best Buy.'
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Single-pool executive comp tied to enterprise results is an observable, filable proxy for whether a company has actually dismantled internal zero-sum behavior.
insights.quote: one team, one dream, one Best Buy
insights.locator: Joly’s second shift at Best Buy

insights.claim: Joly reports the hardest personal change of the Best Buy turnaround was learning to say 'I don't know' and 'I need help', converging with Rometty's conclusion that admitting a limit makes a leader stronger rather than weaker.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Two independent large-cap turnaround CEOs land on the same non-obvious lever — public admission of uncertainty — a signal worth listening for on earnings calls.
insights.quote: the hardest thing he had to learn was to say, “I don’t know” and “I need help.”
insights.locator: This is where Joly and Rometty landed

insights.claim: BCG's read of the Best Buy comeback is that it did not come from working harder at existing beliefs but from the team admitting the market was not the only thing that had to change — and that no single leader can produce that shift alone.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reframes turnaround underwriting: effort and cost-cutting intensity are weak predictors; collective assumption change at the top team is the claimed differentiator.
insights.quote: Joly’s teams didn’t turn Best Buy around by working harder at what they already believed.
insights.locator: Naming beliefs is the easy part

themes.theme: Rometty's IBM Sequence: Story Before System

insights.claim: Ginni Rometty's account of IBM's reinvention is that belief cannot be argued into a team — 'until you experience it, you don't really believe it' — so lasting change begins with lived experience rather than ending with it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Predicts that top-down communication campaigns and mandated frameworks underperform pilot-and-experience rollouts in large-scale corporate transformations.
insights.quote: until you experience it, you don’t really believe it
insights.locator: Why does belief so often determine

insights.claim: To shift how nearly half a million IBM employees worked, Rometty started with three beliefs, translated them into nine behaviors, asked the workforce to define what each looked like at its best, opened every meeting with a story about one behavior, and only afterward hardwired the behaviors into promotion criteria and pulse surveys.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A specific, copyable sequencing template (3 beliefs to 9 behaviors to stories to systems) with an explicit ordering constraint most change programs violate.
insights.quote: A system that is installed before people have lived the belief is easy to ignore. The story has to come first.
insights.locator: Make the new belief experiential, then wire it in

insights.claim: Rometty's method for moving leaders who won't voluntarily step into discomfort was experiential rather than argumentative: draw on the hard things they had already survived to shrink a professional risk by comparison, or talk through the worst-case outcome until it lost its grip, then have them take a small first step and see it hold.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Operational technique for de-risking executive inaction — reframing plus a small reversible step — applicable wherever incumbency inertia is the blocker.
insights.quote: growth and comfort can never coexist
insights.locator: Some leaders won’t step into discomfort

insights.claim: Rometty says her hardest personal shift was accepting that empathy requires vulnerability and that vulnerability builds followership instead of undercutting it — directly contradicting the assumption BCG identifies as the root of the 25-point empathy gap.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Provides the counterexample that breaks the perceived empathy-versus-accountability tradeoff, the specific belief blocking the largest measured capability gap.
insights.locator: For Rometty the hardest shift was accepting

themes.theme: Interventions a Team Can Actually Run

insights.claim: BCG's first prescribed intervention is forcing a team to complete the sentence 'We're doing this because we believe…' before a major decision and to run it backward on decisions that failed — 'We did that because we believed… Was that accurate?' — which frequently exposes assumptions that stopped being true long ago.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A zero-cost pre-mortem/post-mortem protocol that surfaces stale operating assumptions; its absence in a company's decision process is itself a red flag.
insights.quote: Name the belief underlying the decision.
insights.locator: How to Start

insights.claim: BCG recommends polarity workshops to attack false tradeoffs — individualism versus collaboration, strategic clarity versus tolerance for ambiguity — treating opposed sides as a tension to manage rather than a choice to settle, since the right balance shifts with business context.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Names the mechanism by which teams over-index on one pole (e.g. default consensus) and lose speed — a diagnosable cause of slow decision cycles.
insights.locator: Challenge the false tradeoff

insights.claim: BCG argues the productive question for a capability gap is not 'How do we get better at empathy?' but 'What would have to be true for us to exhibit empathy when the pressure is on?', because the blocking belief only shifts once it is stated explicitly.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Reframes capability-gap remediation from training procurement to belief excavation — a cheaper intervention with a claimed larger measured effect.
insights.quote: the right question isn't “How do we get better at empathy?” but “What would have to be true for us to exhibit empathy when the pressure is on?”
insights.locator: Audit the two widest gaps

insights.claim: BCG concedes that naming beliefs is the easy part and that getting a team to examine its own assumptions out loud and admit some no longer fit is the real barrier — 'Most leaders would rather do almost anything else' — implying the prescribed interventions face high adoption failure.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Self-limiting admission worth pricing in: if the intervention is behaviorally aversive, the 15% who complete all three steps is unlikely to expand quickly, preserving the outperformance spread.
insights.quote: Most leaders would rather do almost anything else.
insights.locator: Naming beliefs is the easy part
